new.title: Walk the rainbow on the roof of ARoS
new.desc: ARoS, a ten-storey cube by Schmidt Hammer Lassen that opened in 2004, is one of the largest art museums in Northern Europe. On its roof sits Olafur Eliasson's Your Rainbow Panorama from 2011: a circular glass walkway 150 metres long and 52 metres across, glazed in every colour of the spectrum, so the city outside shifts from red to violet as you walk.
new.tip: The museum stays open until 20:00 on weekdays except Mondays, when it is closed, and the rainbow is at its best at dusk as the lights come on. Leave time for the giant crouching Boy by Ron Mueck on the ground floor.

new.title: Step back in time in Den Gamle By
new.desc: Den Gamle By is an open-air museum of town life, with 75 historic buildings moved here from 20 Danish towns. It began in 1914 with a single house, the Mayor's House from about 1597, still one of the finest half-timbered Renaissance buildings in Denmark, and has since added whole streets from the 1920s and the 1970s.
new.tip: Buy a pastry at the old bakery and peek into the 1970s flats for a dose of nostalgia. In the weeks before Christmas the streets fill with a traditional Christmas market.

new.title: Meet the Grauballe Man at Moesgaard Museum
new.desc: Henning Larsen's 2014 building rises out of the hillside south of the city, with a sloping grass roof you can climb. Inside, the star is the Grauballe Man, called the world's best preserved bog body, alongside runestones and a vast hoard of Iron Age weapons from Illerup Ådal.
new.tip: City buses run from the centre to the door. Afterwards follow the 4 km Prehistoric Trail through woods and reconstructed houses down to Moesgaard beach.

new.title: Find St Christopher in Aarhus Cathedral
new.desc: At about 93 metres long and 96 metres tall, Aarhus Cathedral is the longest and tallest church in Denmark. Its walls carry some 220 square metres of medieval frescoes, more than any other Danish church, including a towering St Christopher, and the gilded altarpiece by Bernt Notke was dedicated on Easter Sunday 1479.
new.tip: Entry is free. Look up for the model ship Enigheden from 1720, the largest church ship in Denmark, hanging in the nave.

new.title: Get lost in the lanes of the Latin Quarter
new.desc: The Latin Quarter behind the cathedral is the oldest part of Aarhus, a knot of cobbled streets such as Badstuegade, Graven and Mejlgade lined with low painted houses. Today it is full of independent shops, cafés and small galleries rather than Latin-speaking scholars.
new.tip: Wander in the late afternoon when the café terraces fill up, and end on Pustervig square for a drink in the sun.

new.title: Stroll Møllestien among the hollyhocks
new.desc: Møllestien is a short cobbled lane of pastel houses, many from the 18th and 19th centuries, with hollyhocks growing up their walls. It was a poor quarter well into the 1960s before artists and students restored the crooked houses.
new.tip: People live here, so keep your voice down. Come in July when the hollyhocks are at full height.

new.title: Circle the Iceberg on Aarhus Ø
new.desc: Isbjerget, the Iceberg, is a jagged white housing block completed in 2013 on the former container harbour of Aarhus Ø. Four firms, CEBRA, JDS, SeARCH and Louis Paillard, shaped its peaks so that every flat gets a view of the bay, with blue glass balconies echoing ice.
new.tip: Walk the waterfront path all the way round the building, then continue to the harbour bath and the Navitas building nearby.

new.title: Hear the birth bell ring in Dokk1
new.desc: Dokk1, opened in 2015 on the old harbour front, is described as the largest public library in Scandinavia and was named the world's Public Library of the Year in 2016. Above the central staircase hangs a 7.5 metre bronze tube bell linked to the university hospital: parents press a button when their baby is born and it rings across the hall.
new.tip: It is free and open long hours, a great rainy day stop. Grab a window seat on the upper floor for views over the harbour and the light rail.

new.title: Watch the guard change at Marselisborg Palace
new.desc: Marselisborg Palace was built in 1899 to 1902 to designs by Hack Kampmann and given by the people of Denmark to Prince Christian and Alexandrine as a wedding present. It is still the royal family's summer home in Jutland.
new.tip: The palace itself never opens, but the park is free when the royals are away. When they are in residence, the changing of the guard takes place at noon.

new.title: Admire Arne Jacobsen's marble city hall
new.desc: Aarhus City Hall, finished in 1941 by Arne Jacobsen and Erik Møller, is clad in 6,000 square metres of grey Norwegian marble from Porsgrunn. Its slim 60 metre tower, with a clock face 7 metres across, was only added after public pressure.
new.tip: Saturday guided tours take you inside and up the clock tower. Outside, look for the pig fountain on City Hall Square.

new.title: Take in the city from Salling Rooftop
new.desc: On top of the Salling department store on the main shopping street, a free rooftop terrace looks out over the cathedral, ARoS and the harbour. A glass walkway sticks out over the edge so you can peer straight down at the shoppers on Søndergade.
new.tip: Head up through the store to the top floor. It closes with the shop, around 20:00 on weekdays and earlier at weekends.

new.title: Walk the circle of the Infinite Bridge
new.desc: Den Uendelige Bro is a round wooden pier, 60 metres across, that reaches out into the bay at Ballehage beach below the Varna Palace. Designed by Niels Povlsgaard and Johan Gjøde for Sculpture by the Sea in 2015, it proved so popular that the city rebuilt it as a permanent work in 2017.
new.tip: Cycle out along the shore from the city centre in about 20 minutes. Sunrise and sunset are magic, and you can swim from the beach right beside it.

new.title: Go down into the crypt of Vor Frue Kirke
new.desc: Beneath the choir of the Church of Our Lady lies a stone crypt church, one of the oldest in Scandinavia, rediscovered during restoration work in 1955. Above ground the church still has its medieval monastery wing with painted vaults.
new.tip: Entry is free. The stairs to the crypt are behind the choir, and it is a cool, quiet escape from the shopping streets on a hot day.
new.q: Vor Frue Kirke, Frue Kirkeplads, Aarhus

new.title: Dive into the harbour bath on Aarhus Ø
new.desc: The Harbour Bath, designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, floats in Bassin 7 with a 50 metre lane pool, a round diving pool, children's pools and saunas. Swimming in clean harbour water is free in summer, with lifeguards on duty.
new.tip: Bring your own padlock for the lockers. Outside summer, the diving pool still opens for winter swimmers on weekend mornings.

new.title: Feed the deer in Marselisborg Deer Park
new.desc: Since 1932 this 22 hectare fenced corner of the Marselisborg forests has been home to free-roaming sika and roe deer, and wild boar in their own enclosure. The deer are so tame they will eat from your hand.
new.tip: Bring carrots or apples, never bread, and do not feed the boar at all. Entry is free from dawn to dusk all year.

new.title: Hike the beech slopes of Riis Skov
new.desc: Riis Skov, an 80 hectare beech wood on the bay north of the centre, was presented to Aarhus in 1395 and is called the first public forest in Denmark. Paths climb and dip through the trees with glimpses of the water below.
new.tip: Walk there along the coast from Aarhus Ø, then come down to the shore for a swim at Den Permanente.

new.title: Swim from the old sea bath at Den Permanente
new.desc: Den Permanente is a wooden sea bath from 1933 at the foot of Riis Skov, with jetties, a small beach and separate areas once kept for men and women. It reopened in June 2024 after a renovation and is free to use.
new.tip: Locals swim here all year round, so do not be surprised by bathers in December. Bring a towel and a thermos.

new.title: Ride the roller coasters at Tivoli Friheden
new.desc: Tivoli Friheden is the city's old-fashioned amusement park, set among the trees on the edge of the Marselisborg forests. It mixes roller coasters and a Ferris wheel with gardens, a haunted house and outdoor concerts.
new.tip: The park is seasonal, so check the calendar before you go. An all-inclusive wristband pays off if you plan more than a few rides.

new.title: Catch a show at Godsbanen
new.desc: Aarhus's old goods station, which handled freight from 1923 to 2000, reopened in 2012 as a cultural centre for theatre, music, film and workshops. Its tilted concrete roof is a public space you can walk right up onto.
new.tip: Check the programme for concerts and theatre, or just climb the roof at sunset and have a drink in the café below.

new.title: Join the party during Aarhus Festuge
new.desc: For ten days at the turn of August and September, Aarhus Festuge takes over the city centre with concerts, street theatre, art in public spaces and food events. In 2027 it runs from 27 August to 5 September.
new.tip: Much of the programme in the streets and squares is free. Book accommodation early, as the city fills up.

new.title: Warm up in the tropical dome of the Botanical Garden
new.desc: The greenhouses of the Aarhus Botanical Garden reopened in 2014 with a glass house and a striking tropical dome made of air-filled foil cushions. Inside, four climate zones take you from rainforest to desert.
new.tip: Entry is free, which makes it the perfect escape on a grey day. Combine it with Den Gamle By right next door.

new.title: Picnic under the oaks of the University Park
new.desc: Aarhus University's campus is laid out around a sloping park of old oaks, lawns and ponds, framed by the yellow brick buildings that give the university its look. The landscaped grounds are open to everyone.
new.tip: On a sunny day join the students on the grass by the ponds, and look in at the free Museum of Ancient Art on the campus.

new.title: Graze your way through Aarhus Street Food
new.desc: Opened in August 2016 in an old garage next to the bus station, Aarhus Street Food packs more than 30 kitchens and bars under one roof. You can eat your way from smørrebrød to dumplings and tacos in one evening.
new.tip: Kitchens are open daily from 11:30 to 21:00. Go early on Friday and Saturday evenings or you will struggle for a table.

new.title: Feast on smørrebrød at Klokken
new.desc: Klokken on Mindegade serves classic Danish lunch in a cosy, old-fashioned room: open sandwiches with pan-fried plaice, roast beef or homemade chicken salad, followed by warm dishes like pork with parsley sauce. Its all-you-can-eat smørrebrød lunch lets you try one topping after another.
new.tip: Pair lunch with a glass of the house schnapps, made with Copenhagen Distillery. Book a table at weekends.

new.title: Grab a cardamom bun at La Cabra
new.desc: La Cabra began as a small roastery in Aarhus and became one of the best known names in Nordic coffee. Its café on Graven in the Latin Quarter serves light-roasted filter coffee alongside sourdough and cardamom buns from its own bakery.
new.tip: Buns tend to sell out by early afternoon, so come in the morning. Take your cup to the steps of the Latin Quarter outside.

new.title: Shop the market on Ingerslevs Boulevard
new.desc: Twice a week, on Wednesday and Saturday mornings, around 60 stalls line the leafy boulevard in Frederiksbjerg. Farmers, cheesemakers, bakers and flower sellers set up between the trees, and many products are homemade.
new.tip: The market runs from 08:00 to 14:00. Saturday is the liveliest, so come early, then have brunch on nearby Jægergårdsgade or M.P. Bruuns Gade.

new.title: Sip craft beer at Mikkeller Bar on Jægergårdsgade
new.desc: Jægergårdsgade in Frederiksbjerg is one of the city's favourite streets for an evening out, and Mikkeller's Aarhus bar is its craft beer anchor, with a long tap list of its own and guest beers.
new.tip: Ask the staff for a taster flight before committing to a full glass. The bar is a short walk from the central station.

new.title: Eat your way around Bazar Vest
new.desc: In a former factory in the western suburb of Gellerup, Bazar Vest is an indoor bazaar of greengrocers, halal butchers, spice traders and small restaurants. It feels a world away from the old town, with Turkish pide, Afghan bread and Middle Eastern sweets.
new.tip: Come hungry and graze from stall to stall. Bus 11 runs from the city centre.

new.title: Breakfast at the city's oldest bakery
new.desc: Schweizerbageriet on M.P. Bruuns Gade has been baking for Aarhus since 1898. Its long-fermented breads come out of stone ovens on site, and it has been voted the city's best bakery several times.
new.tip: Try a kanelsnurre, the Danish cinnamon swirl, with a coffee. Come before 10:00 for the full choice.

new.title: Share plates in the Nicolinehus market hall
new.desc: On the ground floor of the Nicolinehus building on Aarhus Ø, a market hall gathers about a dozen food stalls around a beer, wine and cocktail bar. Choose from oysters, dumplings, falafel or smørrebrød and eat together at shared tables.
new.tip: It is a good dinner stop after a swim at the harbour bath, which is a few minutes' walk away.

new.title: Climb the tower on Himmelbjerget
new.desc: Himmelbjerget, the Sky Mountain, rises 147 metres above sea level and drops steeply to Lake Julsø. On top stands a 25 metre red brick tower from 1875, raised in honour of King Frederik VII, who gave Denmark its constitution in 1849.
new.tip: Climb the tower for the view across the Silkeborg lakes. The most romantic way up is by boat from Silkeborg, then the short steep path from the jetty.

new.title: Explore Asger Jorn's collection in Silkeborg
new.desc: Museum Jorn grew out of the art that Asger Jorn, the CoBrA painter who grew up in Silkeborg, collected and gave to his home town from the 1950s on. Today it holds over 30,000 works, including big Jorn canvases and pieces by his friends from across Europe.
new.tip: Do not miss the huge ceramic walls by Jean Dubuffet and Pierre Alechinsky in the courtyard. The museum sits by the Gudenå, a pleasant riverside walk from the centre.

new.title: Look into the face of the Tollund Man
new.desc: In 1950 peat cutters west of Silkeborg found a man so well preserved they thought he was a recent murder victim. He had died around 400 BC, and his calm face, still wearing a leather cap, is now on show at Museum Silkeborg in the old Hovedgården manor.
new.tip: The Elling Woman, found in the same bog twelve years earlier, is on show in the same museum. Allow an hour; the museum is a short walk from the harbour.

new.title: Board the wooden warship Fregatten Jylland
new.desc: The steam frigate Jylland was launched in 1860 and fought the Austrian navy at the Battle of Heligoland in 1864. Restored and set in a dry dock in Ebeltoft, she is one of the longest wooden ships ever built, and you can explore her from the gun decks to the royal cabin.
new.tip: Combine it with a stroll through Ebeltoft's cobbled old town and its tiny old town hall, a few minutes' walk away.

new.title: Cross the causeway to Kalø castle ruin
new.desc: King Erik Menved built Kalø castle in 1313 on a little island in the bay, joined to the land by a cobbled causeway about 500 metres long. The future Swedish king Gustav Vasa was held prisoner here in 1518 and 1519 before escaping dressed as a peasant.
new.tip: The ruin is free and always open. Walk up to the ruined tower for the view across Kalø Vig to Mols Bjerge, and pack a picnic.

new.title: Do time at Horsens prison museum
new.desc: Horsens State Prison held inmates from 1853 until 2006 and is now Fængslet, billed as the world's largest prison museum. You walk the cell blocks and hear the stories of inmates such as Carl August Lorentzen, who escaped in 1949 through a tunnel he began digging with a spoon.
new.tip: Allow at least two hours. The cell where the escape tunnel started is one of the highlights.

new.title: See the painted walls of Viborg Cathedral
new.desc: Viborg's twin-towered cathedral was rebuilt in Romanesque style and consecrated in 1876 on the site of a church begun around 1130. Between 1900 and 1913 Joakim Skovgaard covered its interior with frescoes of Bible stories that glow in deep blues and golds.
new.tip: Walk around the quiet old streets of the cathedral quarter afterwards, and stop at the Skovgaard Museum on the square to see his sketches.

new.title: Discover Manzoni at HEART in Herning
new.desc: HEART, Herning Museum of Contemporary Art, opened in 2009 in a white building by Steven Holl whose curved roof recalls shirt sleeves, a nod to the town's textile past. Its collection began with shirt maker Aage Damgaard, who invited the Italian artist Piero Manzoni to Herning in 1960 and 1961.
new.tip: The museum sits in Birk Centerpark, where sculptures and the Elia artwork are within walking distance.
new.q: HEART Herning Museum of Contemporary Art

new.title: Climb Elia, the giant black dome in Herning
new.desc: Ingvar Cronhammar's sculpture Elia, inaugurated in 2001, is a black dome 60 metres across with four columns rising 32 metres into the sky. Broad stairs lead up onto the dome, and a central chimney can shoot flames several metres high at random moments.
new.tip: It is free and open at all times. The flames are rare, so treat a burst as a bonus and enjoy the view over the flat Jutland heath instead.

new.title: Look out from Bovbjerg Lighthouse
new.desc: First lit in 1877, the 26 metre Bovbjerg Lighthouse stands on a cliff about 40 metres above the North Sea near Lemvig. Climb the 93 steps to the balcony for a sweeping view along the wild west coast.
new.tip: Walk the cliff path south towards Ferring for the best views of the lighthouse, and warm up at the café afterwards.

new.title: Cross the double moat of Spøttrup castle
new.desc: Spøttrup near Skive is a well-preserved medieval fortress built around 1520 to 1530 for the bishops of Viborg. Its red brick wings are wrapped in a double ring of moats and ramparts meant to keep out cannon fire.
new.tip: Climb the ramparts for the best view of the moats, and leave time for the medieval herb and rose gardens.

new.title: Peek into manor life at Gammel Estrup
new.desc: Gammel Estrup, a red brick Renaissance manor near Auning with roots in a moated fortress from 1490, has been a museum since 1930. Its furnished rooms show how Danish nobility lived through the centuries, and the servants' quarters show the other side.
new.tip: Walk the gardens and the moat after the house, and check the programme for seasonal events in the courtyard.

new.title: Walk the park of Rosenholm Castle
new.desc: Rosenholm, begun in 1559 by Jørgen Rosenkrantz, is a four-winged Renaissance castle surrounded by water near Hornslet. Still owned by the same family, it is called Denmark's oldest family-owned castle.
new.tip: The interior can only be seen on guided tours in high summer, but the castle park is a lovely walk most of the year. The castle has also hosted a Christmas market in December.

new.title: Steam across the lakes on the paddle steamer Hjejlen
new.desc: Hjejlen, launched in 1861, is described as the world's oldest coal-fired paddle steamer still in service. In summer she carries passengers from Silkeborg harbour across the lakes to Himmelbjerget, a trip of about an hour and a quarter.
new.tip: Sailings run from May to September and Hjejlen does not sail every departure, so check the timetable if you want the steamer rather than one of the newer boats.

new.title: Hike to the Bronze Age mounds of Trehøje
new.desc: In the heart of Mols Bjerge National Park, three Bronze Age burial mounds crown a hill about 127 metres high. From the top you look out over four inlets, Kalø, Begtrup, Knebel and Ebeltoft, across rolling heath and grassland.
new.tip: Park at Toggerbo and follow the marked trail up through the heather. Wear proper shoes, as the slopes are steeper than they look.

new.title: Paddle a canoe on the Gudenå from Ry
new.desc: The Gudenå, Denmark's longest river, threads through a chain of lakes between Ry and Silkeborg. From Ry you can paddle across Julsø past Himmelbjerget to Silkeborg, about 19 km in all.
new.tip: Only canoes from approved rental firms are allowed on this stretch, so rent from Ry Kanofart at the marina. Wind can whip up on the big lakes, so keep close to the shore.

new.title: Sweat it out in the domes of Randers Regnskov
new.desc: Randers Regnskov is a tropical zoo in three domes representing South America, Africa and Asia, opened in 1996. More than 175 species live inside, from sloths and monkeys to crocodiles, roaming among the plants in warm, humid air.
new.tip: Dress in layers, as it is hot inside and cold outside. The South America dome is the tallest, at 25 metres.

new.title: Walk the shores of Hald Sø
new.desc: South of Viborg, Hald Sø is one of the deepest lakes in Denmark, ringed by oak forest, heath and the Dollerup hills. The Hald Hovedgård manor and the ruins of medieval castles stand on its banks.
new.tip: Start from Hald Hovedgård and follow the lakeside trail, which takes in the old castle ruins and the views from Dollerup Bakker.

new.title: Walk the memorial valley of Kongenshus heath
new.desc: Kongenshus Mindepark protects some 1,200 hectares of open Jutland heath. In its memorial valley stand 39 district stones ringed by parish stones, carved with the names of about 1,200 settlers who broke this poor soil into farmland.
new.tip: Come in August when the heather is purple. The park is free and always open.

new.title: Scream on the coasters of Djurs Sommerland
new.desc: Djurs Sommerland on Djursland bills itself as the largest amusement park in the Nordic region, with more than 60 rides and a large water park. The season runs from spring until the Halloween weeks in October.
new.tip: Bring swimwear for the water park, which is open in high summer. Arrive at opening to ride the big coasters before the queues build.

new.title: Walk under sharks at Kattegatcentret
new.desc: The aquarium at Grenaa harbour, opened in 1993, is home to more than 250 species from the Kattegat and tropical seas. Its 550,000 litre shark tank has a tunnel where sand tiger and nurse sharks glide over your head.
new.tip: Time your visit with a seal or shark feeding, and check the beach next to the aquarium afterwards.

new.title: Learn to windsurf on Ringkøbing Fjord
new.desc: At Hvide Sande a narrow strip of dunes separates the North Sea from the shallow Ringkøbing Fjord. The flat, waist-deep water of the fjord is a favourite place to learn windsurfing and kitesurfing.
new.tip: Surf schools at Hvide Sande Nord rent gear and give lessons for beginners. Watch out for fishing nets in the fjord.

new.title: Cycle to the bell tower in Nordby on Samsø
new.desc: Nordby, voted Denmark's best-kept village in 1990, has half-timbered farmhouses wrapped around a village pond. Its yellow bell tower from 1857 stands where the farmers once met, and the bells still ring at sunrise and sunset in season.
new.tip: Samsø is flat enough to cycle all over. Rent a bike near the ferry and continue to the hills of Nordby Bakker for the view.

new.title: Eat smoked fish fresh from Hvide Sande harbour
new.desc: Nordsø Fisk sits across from the fish auction hall in Hvide Sande, and most of its catch comes straight from the auction every morning. Fish is salted and smoked by hand in the shop's own smokehouse, several times a day in summer.
new.tip: Order a plate of warm smoked fish or fish and chips at the bistro and eat it by the harbour. It is open all year.

new.title: Buy new potatoes from a Samsø roadside stall
new.desc: Samsø's mild island climate lets farmers dig the first new potatoes in Denmark every May, and they are a national event. In season, dozens of honesty stalls along the roads sell potatoes, strawberries, asparagus and other produce.
new.tip: Bring coins or MobilePay for the honesty boxes. Boil the potatoes simply and eat them with butter, salt and chives.

new.title: Taste island beer at Fur Bryghus
new.desc: The family-run Fur brewery opened in 2004 in a red wooden building from 1926 on the island of Fur in the Limfjord, near the striking moler cliffs. Its restaurant serves seasonal food from local farms with the house beers.
new.tip: Take the five-minute ferry from Branden, then walk the cliffs of Knudeklint before settling in for a tasting.

new.title: Sip farm-brewed beer in Mols Bjerge
new.desc: Ebeltoft Gårdbryggeri brews beer and natural sodas by hand on a farm from 1860 in the village of Hyllested Skovgårde, inside Mols Bjerge National Park. From the café and taproom you look out over the hills and the water.
new.tip: Opening hours vary with the season, so check the brewery's website or social media before you drive out. It pairs well with a hike on the nearby trails.

new.title: Have smørrebrød in Randers' oldest brick house
new.desc: Special Smørrebrød on Rådhustorvet in Randers serves classic open sandwiches, homemade bread and cakes. It is housed in Påskesønnernes Gård, said to be the oldest brick house in town, dating back to 1460.
new.tip: On a sunny day take a table on the square outside. Everything is also available to take away.

new.title: Taste organic cheese at Thise Mejeri
new.desc: Thise Mejeri was founded in 1988 by seven farmers who wanted their own organic dairy, in the buildings of an old village dairy north of Skive. Its cheese, butter and yogurt are now sold all over Denmark, and the dairy shop lets you taste before you buy.
new.tip: Check the opening hours before you go, as they change in summer. Pick up a cheese for a picnic on the Salling peninsula.

new.title: Dine by the beach at Molskroen
new.desc: Molskroen is a seaside inn on Femmøller Strand near Ebeltoft, at the edge of Mols Bjerge National Park. Its kitchen works closely with producers from Mols and Djursland, and Michelin has recognised it with a Green Star for sustainability.
new.tip: Book ahead, especially for dinner in summer, and take an evening walk on the beach afterwards.
